statement: Let $f$ be continuous on the closed strip $S = \{a \le \operatorname{Im} z \le b\}$ and [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) inside, with the [growth](c:growth-order) bound $|f(z)| \le A\exp(B e^{c|\operatorname{Re} z|})$ for some $c < \pi/(b-a)$. If $|f| \le C$ on both boundary lines, then $|f| \le C$ on $S$.

hypotheses.text: The numbers satisfy $a < b$, and $S$ is the closed strip $a \le \operatorname{Im} z \le b$.
The function $f$ is continuous on $S$ and [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) in the open strip $a < \operatorname{Im} z < b$.
Constants $A, B$ and $c < \pi/(b-a)$ give $|f(z)| \le A\exp(B e^{c|\operatorname{Re} z|})$ in the open strip, a [growth](c:growth-order) bound.
The bound $|f(z)| \le C$ holds whenever $\operatorname{Im} z = a$ or $\operatorname{Im} z = b$.

formal.difference: The declaration allows $f$ with values in any complex normed space and states the growth bound only for large $|\operatorname{Re} z|$ in the open strip. It fixes one point $z$ of the closed strip instead of quantifying over $S$.

proofs.name: Damping factor and maximum modulus
proofs.slogan: Damp $f$ by an auxiliary double-exponential factor, apply the maximum modulus principle on a long rectangle, then remove the damping.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for the closed strip with $a < b$. The proof reduces to $C > 0$ and a strip centered on the real axis.

roles.why: The width $b - a$ fixes the critical exponent $\pi/(b-a)$ and the shift of step 1.
Holomorphy inside and continuity up to the boundary allow the maximum modulus principle on the rectangle.
The growth bound has an exponent $c$ below the exponent $d$ of the damping factor, so the damped function decays.
The bound $C$ on the two boundary lines is the boundary value that the maximum principle spreads inside.

steps.slogan: Reduce to $C > 0$ and to a strip centered on the real axis.
steps.detail: The boundary lines are covered by the hypothesis. The boundary bound forces $C \ge 0$, and the claim for every $C' > C$ gives the claim for $C$, so take $C > 0$. Translate by $-i(a+b)/2$, so the strip is $|\operatorname{Im} w| \le \beta$ with $\beta = (b-a)/2$ and $c < \pi/(2\beta)$.

steps.slogan: Choose $d$ with $c < d < \pi/(2\beta)$ and form the damping factors $g_\varepsilon$.
steps.detail: Pick $d$ with $\max(c, 0) < d < \pi/(2\beta)$. For $\varepsilon < 0$ put $g_\varepsilon(w) = \exp(\varepsilon(e^{dw} + e^{-dw})) = \exp(2\varepsilon\cosh(dw))$. This is an entire function and an [exponential](c:exponential-function) of an exponential.

steps.slogan: Bound $|g_\varepsilon|$ by a double-exponential decay inside the strip.
steps.detail: For $w = x + iy$ with $|y| \le \beta$, $\operatorname{Re}\cosh(dw) = \cosh(dx)\cos(dy) \ge \cos(d\beta)\cosh(dx) > 0$, since $d\beta < \pi/2$. So $|g_\varepsilon(w)| \le \exp(\delta e^{d|x|})$ with $\delta = \varepsilon\cos(d\beta) < 0$, and in particular $|g_\varepsilon| \le 1$ on the strip.

steps.slogan: Show that $g_\varepsilon f$ tends to zero at both ends of the strip.
steps.detail: With $R = |\operatorname{Re} w|$, the bounds give $|g_\varepsilon f| \le A\exp(\delta e^{dR} + Be^{cR})$. Since $d > c$ and $\delta < 0$, the exponent tends to $-\infty$. Hence some $R > |\operatorname{Re} z|$ gives $|g_\varepsilon f| \le C$ on the vertical sides $|\operatorname{Re} w| = R$ of the rectangle.

steps.slogan: Bound $g_\varepsilon f$ on the long rectangle by the [maximum modulus principle](c:maximum-modulus).
steps.detail: The function $g_\varepsilon f$ is continuous on the closed rectangle $[-R, R] \times [-\beta, \beta]$ and [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) inside. On the horizontal sides $|g_\varepsilon| \le 1$ and $|f| \le C$; on the vertical sides step 4 gives $\le C$. So $|g_\varepsilon f| \le C$ on the rectangle, in particular at $z$.

steps.slogan: Let $\varepsilon$ tend to $0$ from below to remove the damping.
steps.detail: For each $\varepsilon < 0$, $|g_\varepsilon(z) f(z)| \le C$. As $\varepsilon \to 0^-$, $g_\varepsilon(z) \to 1$, so $|f(z)| \le C$.

concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy of $f$ and of $g_\varepsilon$ allows the maximum modulus principle.
concepts.c:growth-order: The double-exponential growth bound is beaten by the damping factor when $d > c$.
concepts.c:maximum-modulus: The bounded rectangle case is the starting point that the damping extends.
concepts.c:exponential-function: Both the damping factor and the growth bound are doubly exponential.

statement: Let $f(x) = a_n x^n + \dots + a_0$ be a [polynomial](c:polynomial) with [integer](c:integer) coefficients and $a_n \ne 0$. If the [rational number](c:rational-number) $p/q$ with $p, q$ [coprime](c:coprime-integers) and $q > 0$ is a [root](c:root-of-a-polynomial) of $f$, then $p$ [divides](c:divisibility) $a_0$ and $q$ divides $a_n$.

hypotheses.text: The coefficients $a_0, \dots, a_n$ of $f$ are [integers](c:integer) and $a_n \ne 0$.
The rational number $p/q$ is a [root](c:root-of-a-polynomial) of $f$.
The integers $p$ and $q$ are [coprime](c:coprime-integers) and $q > 0$.

conclusion: The integer $p$ divides $a_0$ and the integer $q$ divides $a_n$.

proofs.name: Clearing denominators
proofs.slogan: Multiply the root equation by $q^n$ and read divisibility off the two end terms.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. A polynomial with a root has $n \ge 1$; if $p = 0$ then $a_0 = 0$ and $0$ divides $0$.

roles.why: Integer coefficients make the cleared equation an identity between integers, so divisibility applies.
The root equation $f(p/q) = 0$ is the identity that the proof clears of denominators.
Coprimality lets the proof cancel $q^n$ against $p$ and $p^n$ against $q$.

steps.slogan: Clear denominators by multiplying $f(p/q) = 0$ by $q^n$.
steps.detail: Multiplying $\sum_{k=0}^n a_k (p/q)^k = 0$ by $q^n$ gives the integer identity $a_n p^n + a_{n-1} p^{n-1} q + \dots + a_1 p q^{n-1} + a_0 q^n = 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $p$ divides $a_0 q^n$ and then $a_0$.
steps.detail: Every term except $a_0 q^n$ contains the factor $p$, so $p$ [divides](c:divisibility) $a_0 q^n$. Since $p$ and $q$ are [coprime](c:coprime-integers), so are $p$ and $q^n$, and Euclid's lemma gives $p \mid a_0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $q$ divides $a_n p^n$ and then $a_n$.
steps.detail: Every term except $a_n p^n$ contains the factor $q$, so $q$ divides $a_n p^n$. Since $q$ and $p^n$ are coprime, Euclid's lemma gives $q \mid a_n$.

steps.slogan: Join the two divisibility statements into the theorem.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give $p \mid a_0$ and $q \mid a_n$. If $a_0 = 0$ the first statement reads $p \mid 0$, which always holds.

concepts.c:polynomial: The proof studies one polynomial with integer coefficients and its value at $p/q$.
concepts.c:integer: Integer coefficients and integer $p, q$ make divisibility arguments possible.
concepts.c:rational-number: The root $p/q$ is a fraction, and clearing its denominator is the first step.
concepts.c:coprime-integers: Coprimality of $p$ and $q$ cancels powers of one against the other.
concepts.c:root-of-a-polynomial: The root condition $f(p/q) = 0$ gives the identity that the proof analyzes.
concepts.c:divisibility: Each end term of the identity is divisible by the other number.

source.note: The classical clearing-denominators proof, as in Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra, section 9.4 (the rational root criterion).

statement: Let $U$ be a one-parameter Ad-unipotent subgroup of a connected [Lie group](c:lie-group) $G$, acting on $\Gamma\backslash G$ for a lattice $\Gamma$. Every [ergodic](c:ergodic-measure) $U$-invariant probability measure is the invariant measure of a closed orbit of a closed subgroup $L \supseteq U$, and every $U$-orbit closure is such an orbit.

hypotheses.text: The subgroup $\Gamma$ is a [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup) of $G$, so $\Gamma\backslash G$ is a [homogeneous space](c:homogeneous-space) with a finite measure induced by [Haar measure](c:haar-measure).
The group $U = \{u_t\}$ is a one-parameter subgroup of $G$ with $\mathrm{Ad}(u_t)$ unipotent for every $t$, so $U$ acts on $\Gamma\backslash G$ by a [unipotent flow](c:unipotent-flow).

conclusion: Each ergodic $U$-invariant probability measure is the $L$-invariant measure on a closed $L$-orbit, and each $U$-orbit closure is a closed $L$-orbit, for closed subgroups $L \supseteq U$.

proofs.name: Polynomial divergence and measure classification
proofs.slogan: Use the polynomial divergence of unipotent orbits to classify the invariant ergodic measures, then deduce the orbit closures.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof, which runs to hundreds of pages. Steps 1 to 3 follow the Annals paper and steps 4 to 6 follow the Duke paper; the detail of each step rests on the cited work.

roles.why: Finite volume of $\Gamma\backslash G$ gives the ergodic theorem, and it prevents orbit averages from losing mass.
Unipotence makes the divergence of nearby orbits polynomial, which drives the shearing argument.

steps.slogan: Show that nearby points diverge along $U$ at a polynomial rate.
steps.detail: For $x$ and $xg$ close together, the displacement $u_t^{-1} g u_t = \exp(\mathrm{Ad}(u_{-t}) \log g)$ has Lie algebra coordinates that are polynomials in $t$. Ratner uses this slow divergence where hyperbolic flows diverge exponentially.

steps.slogan: Compare the orbits of two generic nearby points to find a new symmetry of $\mu$.
steps.detail: Take two nearby points that are generic for the [ergodic](c:ergodic-measure) measure $\mu$. After a change of time on the second orbit, their displacement tends to a fixed element that commutes with $U$ and lies outside it. The ergodic theorem turns this into invariance of $\mu$ under a unipotent group $W \not\subseteq U$.

steps.slogan: Repeat the shearing until the invariance group is maximal and the measure is homogeneous.
steps.detail: Iterating with $\langle U, W \rangle$ in place of $U$ ends at the largest closed subgroup $\Lambda$ that preserves $\mu$. Ratner's measure classification then shows that $\mu$ is the finite $\Lambda$-invariant measure on a closed orbit $x\Lambda$.

steps.slogan: Show that orbit averages of $U$ keep their mass inside compact sets.
steps.detail: Because $\Gamma\backslash G$ has finite volume, the non-divergence results of Dani and Margulis keep a fixed share of each long $U$-orbit segment in a compact set. So weak limits of orbit averages are probability measures.

steps.slogan: Identify every limit of orbit averages with a homogeneous measure.
steps.detail: A weak limit of $U$-orbit averages is $U$-invariant, so its ergodic components are homogeneous by step 3. The Duke paper combines this with the algebraic structure of the orbit closures to show that the limit is the measure of one closed orbit $xL$.

steps.slogan: Read the orbit closure and the invariant measures off the classified limits.
steps.detail: The support of the limit is a closed orbit $xL$ with $L \supseteq U$ closed, and the orbit averages of $x$ equidistribute in it. So the closure of $xU$ equals $xL$, and step 3 gives the measure statement.

concepts.c:lie-group: The group $G$ carries the Lie algebra in which the divergence is computed.
concepts.c:ergodic-measure: Ergodic measures are the building blocks that the classification describes.
concepts.c:lattice-discrete-subgroup: A lattice gives finite volume, which controls the ergodic theorem and non-divergence.
concepts.c:homogeneous-space: The quotient $\Gamma\backslash G$ and the closed orbits $xL$ are homogeneous spaces.
concepts.c:haar-measure: Haar measure induces the finite invariant measure on the quotient by the lattice.
concepts.c:unipotent-flow: The flow of $U$ has polynomial orbit divergence, the key input of the proof.

source.ref: M. Ratner, On Raghunathan's measure conjecture, Annals of Mathematics 134 (1991), 545-607; and M. Ratner, Raghunathan's topological conjecture and distributions of unipotent flows, Duke Mathematical Journal 63 (1991), 235-280
source.note: The Annals paper proves the measure classification; the Duke paper proves the orbit closure and equidistribution theorems.

statement: Let $\sum a_n$ be a [conditionally convergent](c:conditional-convergence) real [series](c:series). For all $-\infty \le \alpha \le \beta \le \infty$, some rearrangement of its terms has partial sums $s_n$ with $\liminf s_n = \alpha$ and $\limsup s_n = \beta$. So a rearrangement converges to any chosen real number, and another diverges.

hypotheses.text: The [series](c:series) $\sum a_n$ of real numbers converges.
The series $\sum |a_n|$ diverges, so the convergence is not [absolute](c:absolute-convergence).
The numbers $\alpha, \beta$ satisfy $-\infty \le \alpha \le \beta \le +\infty$.

conclusion: Some [permutation](c:permutation) $\sigma$ of $\mathbb{N}$ gives [partial sums](c:partial-sum) $s_n$ of $\sum a_{\sigma(n)}$ with $\liminf s_n = \alpha$ and $\limsup s_n = \beta$.

proofs.name: Greedy rearrangement
proofs.slogan: Rearrange the terms greedily so that the partial sums swing between targets that approach the two limits.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for real, infinite and equal targets. Taking $\alpha = \beta = L$ gives convergence to $L$, taking $\alpha = \beta = \pm\infty$ gives divergence to $\pm\infty$, and $\alpha < \beta$ gives oscillation.

roles.why: Convergence forces $a_n \to 0$, so the overshoot at every turning point is small.
Divergence of $\sum |a_n|$ makes both the nonnegative part and the negative part diverge.
The two numbers fix the levels that the swinging partial sums approach.

steps.slogan: Split the terms into a nonnegative list $P_j$ and a negative list $-Q_j$.
steps.detail: The sums $\sum p_n$ and $\sum q_n$ diverge, where $p_n = (|a_n| + a_n)/2$ and $q_n = (|a_n| - a_n)/2$: otherwise $\sum |a_n|$ converges or $\sum a_n$ diverges. So the nonnegative terms $P_1, P_2, \dots$ and the absolute values $Q_1, Q_2, \dots$ of the negative terms form two infinite lists with divergent sums and limit $0$.

steps.slogan: Choose target levels $\alpha_n \to \alpha$ and $\beta_n \to \beta$ with $\alpha_n < \beta_n$ and $\beta_1 > 0$.
steps.detail: Such sequences exist for every choice $-\infty \le \alpha \le \beta \le \infty$, also with $\alpha_n < \beta_{n+1}$, so each stage starts below the next upper target. Infinite limits and $\alpha = \beta$ are allowed.

steps.slogan: Add nonnegative terms until the sum exceeds $\beta_n$, then add negative terms until it falls below $\alpha_n$.
steps.detail: Stage $n$ takes the next unused $P_j$ until the sum exceeds $\beta_n$, then the next unused $Q_j$ until it drops below $\alpha_n$; both stops occur because the two lists have divergent sums. Each stage uses at least one term of each list, so every term appears exactly once and the new series is a [permutation](c:permutation) of the old.

steps.slogan: Bound the overshoot at each turning point by a single term.
steps.detail: Let $x_n$ and $y_n$ be the sums at the ends of the nonnegative and negative runs of stage $n$. By minimality $\beta_n < x_n \le \beta_n + P_{m_n}$ and $\alpha_n - Q_{k_n} \le y_n < \alpha_n$. Since $P_j, Q_j \to 0$, we get $x_n \to \beta$ and $y_n \to \alpha$.

steps.slogan: Locate every partial sum between two turning values to read off the limit inferior and superior.
steps.detail: In stage $n$ the [partial sums](c:partial-sum) rise from $y_{n-1}$ to $x_n$ and then fall to $y_n$, so they stay between $\min(y_{n-1}, y_n)$ and $x_n$. With $y_n \to \alpha$ and $x_n \to \beta$ this gives $\liminf s_n \ge \alpha$ and $\limsup s_n \le \beta$, and the turning sums give equality.

concepts.c:conditional-convergence: Convergence without absolute convergence is exactly what makes rearrangement possible.
concepts.c:series: The theorem rearranges the terms of one real series.
concepts.c:absolute-convergence: Failure of absolute convergence makes both signed parts diverge.
concepts.c:permutation: The greedy construction uses every term once, so it is a permutation.
concepts.c:partial-sum: The partial sums of the new series swing between the targets.

source.note: The classical greedy construction, as in Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, theorem 3.54.

statement: Let $E \to X$ be a complex [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) of rank $n$ over a paracompact Hausdorff space $X$. There is an iterated projective bundle $p\colon F \to X$ (a [flag bundle](c:flag-bundle) of $E$) such that $p^*E$ is a direct sum of $n$ [line bundles](c:line-bundle) and $p^*\colon H^*(X) \to H^*(F)$ is injective on integral [cohomology](c:cohomology).

hypotheses.text: The map $E \to X$ is a complex [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) of rank $n \ge 1$.
The base $X$ is a [paracompact](c:paracompact-space) Hausdorff space.

conclusion: A map $p\colon F \to X$ exists such that $p^*E$ is a sum of line bundles and $p^*$ is injective on $H^*(-;\mathbb{Z})$.

proofs.name: Iterated projective bundles
proofs.slogan: Split off one line bundle on the projective bundle, then repeat on the complement.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, by induction on the rank $n$. The case $n = 1$ takes $F = X$ and $p = \mathrm{id}$.

roles.why: The fibers $\mathbb{C}^n$ give projective bundle fibers $\mathbb{CP}^{n-1}$ and a complement of rank $n - 1$.
Paracompactness gives a Hermitian metric for the complement and keeps the projective bundle paracompact.

steps.slogan: Split a line bundle off the pullback of $E$ to its projective bundle.
steps.detail: Let $q\colon P(E) \to X$ be the [projective bundle](c:projective-bundle) of lines in the fibers. On $P(E)$ the tautological [line bundle](c:line-bundle) $L \subset q^*E$ has an orthogonal complement $E'$ for a Hermitian metric, so $q^*E \cong L \oplus E'$ with $E'$ of rank $n - 1$.

steps.slogan: Show that $q^*$ is injective on cohomology by the Leray-Hirsch theorem.
steps.detail: Let $x = c_1(L^*) \in H^2(P(E))$. On each fiber $\mathbb{CP}^{n-1}$ the classes $1, x, \dots, x^{n-1}$ restrict to a basis of the [cohomology](c:cohomology) of the fiber. So $H^*(P(E))$ is a free $H^*(X)$-module on them, and since $1$ is a basis element, $q^*$ is injective.

steps.slogan: Apply the induction hypothesis to the rank $n - 1$ bundle $E'$ over $P(E)$.
steps.detail: The space $P(E)$ is paracompact Hausdorff, because $q$ is proper with compact fibers over a paracompact base. So some map $r\colon F \to P(E)$ makes $r^*E'$ a sum of $n - 1$ line bundles and makes $r^*$ injective on cohomology.

steps.slogan: Compose the two maps and pull the splitting back to $F$.
steps.detail: Put $p = q \circ r$. Then $p^*E = r^*(L \oplus E') = r^*L \oplus r^*E'$ is a sum of $n$ line bundles, and $p^* = r^* q^*$ is injective as a composite of injective maps.

concepts.c:vector-bundle: The theorem splits a vector bundle into line bundles after pullback.
concepts.c:flag-bundle: The iterated projective bundle $F$ is a flag bundle of $E$.
concepts.c:line-bundle: The tautological line bundle is the summand that splits off at each stage.
concepts.c:cohomology: Injectivity on cohomology transfers identities from $F$ back to $X$.
concepts.c:paracompact-space: Paracompactness supplies Hermitian metrics and survives the passage to $P(E)$.
concepts.c:projective-bundle: The projective bundle carries the tautological line and has fiber $\mathbb{CP}^{n-1}$.

source.note: The classical proof by projective bundles and the Leray-Hirsch theorem, as in Hatcher, Vector Bundles and K-Theory, chapter 3, and Bott and Tu, Differential Forms in Algebraic Topology, section 21.

statement: Let $p_1, p_2, p_3$ be points of a [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) with $p_2 \ne p_1$. Then the [angles](c:angle) of the triangle sum to $\pi$: $\angle p_1 p_2 p_3 + \angle p_2 p_3 p_1 + \angle p_3 p_1 p_2 = \pi$.

hypotheses.text: The points lie in a [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space), a real inner product space acting on an affine space.
The vertices satisfy $p_2 \ne p_1$.

conclusion: $\angle p_1 p_2 p_3 + \angle p_2 p_3 p_1 + \angle p_3 p_1 p_2 = \pi$.

formal.difference: The declaration holds in any real inner product space, also of infinite dimension. It allows degenerate triangles with the convention that an angle with a zero vector equals $\pi/2$.

proofs.name: Splitting of a vector angle
proofs.slogan: Reduce to vectors, split an angle into two parts by comparing cosines and sines, and rearrange.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, degenerate triangles included, with the convention that an angle with a zero vector equals $\pi/2$. The cases $u = 0$ and $u = -y$ of the splitting are direct.

roles.why: The inner product defines $\cos\angle(u,v) = \langle u,v\rangle/(\|u\|\|v\|)$ and gives the Cauchy-Schwarz bound.
The condition $p_2 \ne p_1$ gives $y \ne 0$, the only non-degeneracy that the splitting needs.

steps.slogan: Write each vertex angle as an angle between two difference vectors.
steps.detail: Put $x = p_3 - p_1$ and $y = p_2 - p_1$, so $y \ne 0$ and $x - y = p_3 - p_2$. An [angle](c:angle) between two vectors does not change when both are negated, so the vertex angles are $\angle(x,y)$, $\angle(x,x-y)$ and $\angle(y,y-x)$. The goal is that these three sum to $\pi$.

steps.slogan: Compare the [cosine](c:cosine) and the sine of an angle with those of the sum of its two parts.
steps.detail: For $y \ne 0$ and any $u$, let $\theta = \angle(u,y)$ and $\varphi = \angle(u,u+y) + \angle(y,u+y)$. Write $\cos$ through inner products, and $\sin = \sqrt{1 - \cos^2}$, real by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. The addition formula then gives $\cos\theta = \cos\varphi$ and $\sin\theta = \sin\varphi$, so $\theta \equiv \varphi \pmod{2\pi}$.

steps.slogan: Rule out nonzero multiples of $2\pi$ by the ranges of the angles.
steps.detail: Here $\theta \in [0,\pi]$ and $\varphi \in [0,2\pi]$, so $\theta = \varphi$ unless $\varphi = 2\pi$ and $\theta = 0$. In that case both parts equal $\pi$, so $u = -r(u+y)$ and $y = -s(u+y)$ with $r, s > 0$, and $(1+r+s)(u+y) = 0$ forces $u + y = 0$, which contradicts the angle $\pi$ with $u + y$. Hence $\theta = \varphi$.

steps.slogan: Apply the splitting to $u = x - y$ to relate the three vertex angles.
steps.detail: Since $(x - y) + y = x$, the splitting reads $\angle(x-y, y) = \angle(x-y, x) + \angle(y, x)$.

steps.slogan: Turn the supplement rule and symmetry into the angle sum $\pi$.
steps.detail: Negating one vector gives $\angle(y, x-y) = \pi - \angle(y, y-x)$, and angles are symmetric. So step 4 becomes $\pi - \angle(y,y-x) = \angle(x,x-y) + \angle(x,y)$, which is the goal of step 1.

concepts.c:euclidean-space: The inner product of the space defines angles and the Cauchy-Schwarz bound.
concepts.c:angle: Angles at the vertices become angles between difference vectors.
concepts.c:cosine: Equal cosine and sine make two angles agree modulo $2\pi$.

statement: Every [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve) $E$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is modular: with $N$ its conductor, there is a weight 2 newform $f$ of level $N$ (a [modular form](c:modular-form)) with $L(E,s) = L(f,s)$, equivalently a nonconstant morphism $X_0(N) \to E$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.

hypotheses.text: The curve $E$ is an [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve) defined over $\mathbb{Q}$, with conductor $N$.

conclusion: A weight 2 newform of level $N$ has the same $L$-function as $E$, equivalently a nonconstant morphism $X_0(N) \to E$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ exists.

proofs.name: Modularity lifting
proofs.slogan: Show that the Galois representation of the curve is modular by Taylor-Wiles patching, then read off the newform.
proofs.scope: An outline of the proof of the modularity theorem for every elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$, which this record duplicates. Every step rests on the cited papers of Wiles, Taylor-Wiles and Breuil-Conrad-Diamond-Taylor.

roles.why: The curve supplies its $\ell$-adic [Galois representation](c:galois-representation), whose modularity is the content of the proof.

steps.slogan: Restate the conjecture as the modularity theorem for the Galois representation of $E$.
steps.detail: The conjecture is the modularity theorem for every elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$. It is enough to show that the $\ell$-adic [Galois representation](c:galois-representation) $\rho_{E,\ell}$ comes from a modular form for one prime $\ell$.

steps.slogan: Show that the residual representation modulo $3$ or modulo $5$ is modular.
steps.detail: If $\bar\rho_{E,3}$ is irreducible, the Langlands-Tunnell theorem makes it modular, because its image is solvable. Otherwise $\bar\rho_{E,5}$ is irreducible, and the Wiles $3$-$5$ switch finds a modular curve with the same mod $5$ representation and irreducible mod $3$ representation.

steps.slogan: Set up the universal deformation ring $R$ and the Hecke algebra $\mathbb{T}$ for the residual representation.
steps.detail: The ring $R$ parametrizes lifts of $\bar\rho$ with prescribed ramification and prescribed behavior at $\ell$. The [Hecke algebra](c:hecke-algebra) $\mathbb{T}$ acts on the matching space of [modular forms](c:modular-form), and an isomorphism $R \to \mathbb{T}$ makes every such lift modular.

steps.slogan: Prove $R = \mathbb{T}$ by Taylor-Wiles patching and a numerical criterion.
steps.detail: Auxiliary primes let Taylor and Wiles patch the modules of modular forms. This reduces $R = \mathbb{T}$ to an inequality between a congruence module and a tangent space, which they verify for semistable curves.

steps.slogan: Extend the lifting theorem to potentially Barsotti-Tate representations with wild ramification at 3.
steps.detail: Breuil, Conrad, Diamond and Taylor prove the lifting theorem for representations that are potentially Barsotti-Tate at $3$, using Breuil's description of finite flat group schemes. With the switch of step 2, this covers every elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$.

steps.slogan: Pass from a modular $\rho_{E,\ell}$ to the newform and the parametrization $X_0(N) \to E$.
steps.detail: A modular $\rho_{E,\ell}$ comes from a weight 2 newform $f$ whose level is the conductor $N$ and whose $L$-function equals $L(E,s)$. The Eichler-Shimura construction and Faltings' isogeny theorem then give a nonconstant map $X_0(N) \to E$.

concepts.c:elliptic-curve: The curve is the object whose modularity is proved.
concepts.c:modular-form: The newform $f$ is the modular form that matches the curve.
concepts.c:galois-representation: Modularity of the Galois representation is the reformulation that the proof establishes.
concepts.c:hecke-algebra: The Hecke algebra $\mathbb{T}$ is the modular side of the isomorphism $R = \mathbb{T}$.

source.ref: C. Breuil, B. Conrad, F. Diamond and R. Taylor, On the modularity of elliptic curves over Q: wild 3-adic exercises, Journal of the American Mathematical Society 14 (2001), 843-939
source.note: Completes the proof begun by A. Wiles, Modular elliptic curves and Fermat's last theorem, and R. Taylor and A. Wiles, Ring-theoretic properties of certain Hecke algebras, both Annals of Mathematics 141 (1995).

statement: Let $X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^n$ be a smooth [projective variety](c:projective-variety) over an [algebraically closed field](c:algebraically-closed-field). The hyperplanes $H$ that do not contain $X$ and cut $X$ in a smooth [hyperplane section](c:hyperplane-section) $H \cap X$ contain a dense open subset of the dual projective space $\mathbb{P}^{n*}$.

hypotheses.text: The set $X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^n$ is a smooth [projective variety](c:projective-variety) of dimension $d$.
The ground field $k$ is [algebraically closed](c:algebraically-closed-field), of any characteristic.

conclusion: A dense open set $U \subseteq \mathbb{P}^{n*}$ exists such that each $H \in U$ does not contain $X$ and $H \cap X$ is smooth.

proofs.name: Incidence variety and dimension count
proofs.slogan: Bound the dimension of the set of bad pairs of a point and a hyperplane, then project it to the dual space.
proofs.scope: Smoothness of the section only. Over an algebraically closed field, smooth means regular at every closed point; the connectedness of $H \cap X$ for $\dim X \ge 2$ is a separate theorem and is not proved here.

roles.why: Smoothness of $X$ makes the local rings regular and the first-order jets a bundle of rank $d + 1$.
Over an algebraically closed field the closed points are the $k$-points, and smooth means regular at them.

steps.slogan: Rewrite failure of the section to be regular at $x$ as vanishing of a first-order jet.
steps.detail: Let $h$ define $H$, with local equation $h_x \in \mathcal{O}_{X,x}$. The ring $\mathcal{O}_{X,x}$ is a [regular local ring](c:is-regular-local-ring) of dimension $d$, so the quotient by $h_x$ is regular exactly when $h_x \notin \mathfrak{m}_x^2$. If $h_x \in \mathfrak{m}_x^2$, then either $h_x = 0$ and $X \subseteq H$ near $x$, or the quotient has dimension $d - 1$ and embedding dimension $d$.

steps.slogan: Show that the bad hyperplanes at a point form a linear subspace of codimension $d + 1$.
steps.detail: Let $V = H^0(\mathbb{P}^n, \mathcal{O}(1))$, of dimension $n + 1$. The linear map $V \to \mathcal{O}_X(1)_x / \mathfrak{m}_x^2 \mathcal{O}_X(1)_x$ is onto, because linear forms give all first-order jets on $\mathbb{P}^n$. The target has dimension $1 + d$, so the kernel $B_x$ has dimension $n - d$, and the bad hyperplanes form a projective space of dimension $n - d - 1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the set $B$ of bad pairs $(x, H)$ is closed in $X \times \mathbb{P}^{n*}$.
steps.detail: The universal linear form is a section of $\mathrm{pr}_1^* P^1(\mathcal{O}_X(1)) \otimes \mathrm{pr}_2^* \mathcal{O}(1)$, where $P^1$ is the rank $d + 1$ [bundle of first-order jets](c:jet-bundle) on the smooth variety $X$. Its value at $(x, H)$ is the $1$-jet of $h$ at $x$, so the zero locus $B$ is closed.

steps.slogan: Bound the dimension of $B$ by $n - 1$ using its fibers over $X$.
steps.detail: Over every closed point $x$ the fiber of $B \to X$ is the projective space of $B_x$, of dimension $n - d - 1$. Each irreducible component of $B$ maps onto a closed subset $Y \subseteq X$, so it has dimension at most $\dim Y + n - d - 1 \le n - 1$. If $d = n$, the set $B$ is empty.

steps.slogan: Project $B$ to the dual space to get a proper closed subset.
steps.detail: Since $X$ is projective, the projection $B \to \mathbb{P}^{n*}$ is a closed map, so its image $\Sigma$ is closed. Its dimension is at most $n - 1 < n$, so $U = \mathbb{P}^{n*} \setminus \Sigma$ is open and dense in the irreducible space $\mathbb{P}^{n*}$.

concepts.c:projective-variety: Projectivity of $X$ makes the projection of the bad set to the dual space closed.
concepts.c:algebraically-closed-field: It identifies closed points with $k$-points and smoothness with regularity.
concepts.c:hyperplane-section: The proof shows that a general hyperplane section $H \cap X$ is smooth.
concepts.c:is-regular-local-ring: Regularity of the local ring turns smoothness of the section into a first-order condition.
concepts.c:jet-bundle: The bad pairs are the zeros of a section of a first-order jet bundle.

statement: Let $f\colon X \to Y$ be a continuous map of locally compact Hausdorff spaces such that $f_!$ has finite cohomological dimension. On bounded [derived categories](c:derived-category) of sheaves, $Rf_!$ has a right [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) $f^!$, and $R\mathcal{H}om(Rf_!F, G) \cong Rf_*R\mathcal{H}om(F, f^!G)$ for all $F, G$.

hypotheses.text: The spaces $X$ and $Y$ are locally compact Hausdorff, and $f\colon X \to Y$ is continuous.
The functor $f_!$ on sheaves of abelian groups has finite cohomological dimension.

conclusion: The functor $Rf_!\colon D^b(X) \to D^b(Y)$ has a right adjoint $f^!$, and $R\mathcal{H}om(Rf_!F, G) \cong Rf_*R\mathcal{H}om(F, f^!G)$ in $D^b(Y)$.

proofs.name: Right adjoint of compactly supported pushforward
proofs.slogan: Build the right adjoint of the proper pushforward on injectives, then twist the adjunction by open sets.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof, for sheaves of abelian groups. Each step rests on the cited construction of $f^!$ in Verdier's theory as presented by Kashiwara and Schapira.

roles.why: Local compactness gives $c$-soft resolutions and the functor $f_!$ of sections with proper support.
Finite cohomological dimension keeps $Rf_!$ and $f^!$ on bounded complexes.

steps.slogan: Compute $Rf_!$ with $c$-soft resolutions of finite length.
steps.detail: On locally compact spaces every sheaf has a resolution by $c$-soft sheaves, and $c$-soft sheaves are $f_!$-acyclic. Finite cohomological dimension of $f_!$ makes $Rf_!$ a well-defined functor $D^b(X) \to D^b(Y)$ of [derived categories](c:derived-category).

steps.slogan: Construct $f^!$ on injective sheaves from sections of $f_!$ over open sets.
steps.detail: For an injective sheaf $G$ on $Y$, define $f^!G$ by the Yoneda formula $\Gamma(U; f^!G) = \mathrm{Hom}(f_!\mathbb{Z}_U, G)$ for $U \subseteq X$ open, with $\mathbb{Z}_U$ the extension by zero. One checks that this presheaf is a sheaf.

steps.slogan: Check that $f^!$ is right [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) to $Rf_!$ on derived categories.
steps.detail: Resolve $F$ by $c$-soft sheaves and $G$ by injectives. Then $\mathrm{Hom}(f_!F, G) = \mathrm{Hom}(F, f^!G)$ on complexes, which gives $R\mathrm{Hom}(Rf_!F, G) \cong R\mathrm{Hom}(F, f^!G)$ with bounded complexes by finiteness of dimension.

steps.slogan: Twist the adjunction by open subsets $V \subseteq Y$ with the projection formula.
steps.detail: The projection formula $Rf_!(F \otimes f^{-1}\mathbb{Z}_V) \cong Rf_!F \otimes \mathbb{Z}_V$ lets one replace $F$ by $F \otimes f^{-1}\mathbb{Z}_V$ in the adjunction of step 3, for every open $V \subseteq Y$.

steps.slogan: Read off the isomorphism of sheaves of homomorphisms from sections over every open set.
steps.detail: Step 4 gives $R\Gamma(V; R\mathcal{H}om(Rf_!F, G)) \cong R\Gamma(f^{-1}V; R\mathcal{H}om(F, f^!G))$ for every open $V$. The right side is $R\Gamma(V; Rf_*R\mathcal{H}om(F, f^!G))$, so the two sheaf complexes agree. This is the duality at the core of the [six operations](c:six-operations).

concepts.c:derived-category: Both $Rf_!$ and its adjoint $f^!$ live on bounded derived categories.
concepts.c:adjoint-functor: The existence of $f^!$ is the existence of a right adjoint of $Rf_!$.
concepts.c:six-operations: The isomorphism is the duality statement of the six operations formalism.

source.ref: M. Kashiwara and P. Schapira, Sheaves on Manifolds, Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften 292, Springer, 1990, chapter III, section 3.1
source.note: Verdier's original construction is in J.-L. Verdier, Dualité dans la cohomologie des espaces localement compacts, Séminaire Bourbaki 300 (1965).

statement: Let $M$ be a connected [closed manifold](c:closed-manifold), smooth of dimension $n$. Unique classes $v_k \in H^k(M;\mathbb{F}_2)$ satisfy $\mathrm{Sq}^k x = v_k \smile x$ for all $x \in H^{n-k}(M;\mathbb{F}_2)$, and the total [Stiefel-Whitney class](c:stiefel-whitney-class) of $TM$ equals $\mathrm{Sq}(v) = \sum_k \mathrm{Sq}^k(v)$, where $\mathrm{Sq}^k$ is a [Steenrod square](c:steenrod-square).

hypotheses.text: The space $M$ is a connected [closed manifold](c:closed-manifold) with a smooth structure, of dimension $n$.

proofs.name: Thom class and Pontryagin-Thom collapse
proofs.slogan: Evaluate Steenrod squares of Thom classes on the collapse map, then invert using Poincaré duality.
proofs.scope: Connected $M$; for a disconnected $M$ apply the result to each component. Write $\langle y \rangle$ for the degree $n$ component of $y \in H^*(M;\mathbb{F}_2)$, read as an element of $\mathbb{F}_2$.

roles.why: Compactness gives the collapse map and the fundamental class, and connectedness gives $H^n(M;\mathbb{F}_2) = \mathbb{F}_2$.

steps.slogan: Define the Wu classes by Poincaré duality.
steps.detail: The pairing $H^k \times H^{n-k} \to \mathbb{F}_2$ by the [cup product](c:cup-product) is perfect. The map $x \mapsto \langle \mathrm{Sq}^k x \rangle$ is linear on $H^{n-k}$, so a unique $v_k$ has $\mathrm{Sq}^k x = v_k \smile x$. Then $\langle \mathrm{Sq}(z) \rangle = \langle v z \rangle$ for all $z \in H^*(M;\mathbb{F}_2)$.

steps.slogan: Embed $M$ in Euclidean space and use the Thom class of its normal bundle.
steps.detail:
Embed $M \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ with [normal bundle](c:normal-bundle) $
u$ and Thom class $U$. Thom's definition of Stiefel-Whitney classes gives $\mathrm{Sq}(U) =  ar w \smile U$ with $ ar w = w(
u)$. Since $TM \oplus 
u$ is trivial, $ ar w \, w(TM) = 1$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\mathrm{Sq}^j(x \smile U)$ vanishes for $x \in H^{n-j}(M)$ and $j > 0$.
steps.detail: The Pontryagin-Thom collapse $c\colon S^{n+k} \to T\nu$ has $c^*(aU) = \langle a \rangle$ times the generator. For $j > 0$, $c^*\mathrm{Sq}^j(xU) = \mathrm{Sq}^j c^*(xU) = 0$, because $H^{n+k-j}(S^{n+k})$ is zero or has degree below $j$. So $\mathrm{Sq}^j(xU) = aU$ with $\langle a \rangle = 0$, hence $a = 0$.

steps.slogan: Expand $\mathrm{Sq}(xU)$ by the Cartan formula to get $\langle \mathrm{Sq}(x)\,\bar w \rangle = \langle x \rangle$.
steps.detail: The Cartan formula gives $\mathrm{Sq}(xU) = \mathrm{Sq}(x)\,\bar w\,U$. Its top component vanishes for $\deg x < n$ by step 3 and equals $xU$ for $\deg x = n$. So $\langle \mathrm{Sq}(x)\,\bar w \rangle = \langle x \rangle$ for every $x \in H^*(M;\mathbb{F}_2)$.

steps.slogan: Write $\bar w = \mathrm{Sq}(t)$ and use the Wu classes to get $v \smile t = 1$.
steps.detail: By the Cartan formula $\mathrm{Sq}$ is a ring automorphism, so $\bar w = \mathrm{Sq}(t)$ for a unique $t$. Then $\mathrm{Sq}(x)\,\bar w = \mathrm{Sq}(xt)$, and step 1 gives $\langle \mathrm{Sq}(xt) \rangle = \langle v t x \rangle$. So $\langle v t x \rangle = \langle x \rangle$ for all $x$, and Poincaré duality gives $v t = 1$.

steps.slogan: Invert to obtain $w(TM) = \mathrm{Sq}(v)$.
steps.detail: From $vt = 1$ we get $t = v^{-1}$, so $\bar w = \mathrm{Sq}(v^{-1}) = \mathrm{Sq}(v)^{-1}$. Since $\bar w \, w(TM) = 1$ by step 2, $w(TM) = \mathrm{Sq}(v)$.

concepts.c:closed-manifold: Compactness without boundary gives the fundamental class and the collapse map.
concepts.c:stiefel-whitney-class: Thom's definition of these classes through Steenrod squares is the starting point.
concepts.c:steenrod-square: Steenrod squares define the Wu classes and satisfy the Cartan formula.
concepts.c:cup-product: The cup product pairing is perfect, which defines the Wu classes.
concepts.c:normal-bundle: The normal bundle carries the Thom class and has inverse total class to $TM$.

source.note: The proof of Milnor and Stasheff, Characteristic Classes, section 11 (Wu's formula), by the Thom class of the normal bundle and the Cartan formula.

statement: Let $D \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ be open and connected, and let $A\colon D \to B(H)$ be an [analytic family](c:analytic-family) of [compact operators](c:compact-operator) on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$. Then either $I - A(z)$ is invertible for no $z \in D$, or it is invertible for all $z$ outside a discrete subset of $D$.

hypotheses.text: The set $D \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is open and connected.
The map $A\colon D \to B(H)$ is an [analytic family](c:analytic-family) of bounded operators, analytic in the operator norm.
Each $A(z)$ is a [compact operator](c:compact-operator) on the [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$.

conclusion: Either $I - A(z)$ is never invertible, or a discrete set $S \subset D$ exists with $I - A(z)$ invertible off $S$, $(I - A(z))^{-1}$ [meromorphic](c:meromorphic-function) with finite-rank residues, and $\ker(I - A(z)) \ne 0$ on $S$.

proofs.name: Finite-rank reduction and determinant
proofs.slogan: Reduce locally to a finite-rank perturbation of the identity, study its determinant, and join the local cases by connectedness.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The dichotomy is local first, on a small disc around each point, and then global because $D$ is connected.

roles.why: Connectedness joins the local alternatives into one global alternative.
Analyticity makes the Neumann inverse, the matrix $M(z)$ and its determinant analytic.
A compact operator is a norm limit of finite-rank operators, which starts the reduction.

steps.slogan: Approximate $A(z_0)$ in norm by a finite-rank operator $F$.
steps.detail: A [compact operator](c:compact-operator) on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) is a norm limit of finite-rank operators. Choose $F$ with $\|A(z_0) - F\| < 1/2$. By norm continuity of $A$, a disc $\Omega$ around $z_0$ has $\|A(z) - F\| < 1$ for $z \in \Omega$.

steps.slogan: Factor $I - A(z)$ into an invertible analytic factor and $I$ minus a finite-rank operator.
steps.detail: Put $g(z) = A(z) - F$. Since $\|g(z)\| < 1$, the Neumann series makes $I - g(z)$ invertible with analytic inverse. Then $I - A(z) = (I - g(z))(I - K(z))$, where $K(z) = (I - g(z))^{-1}F$ has finite rank and is analytic.

steps.slogan: Reduce invertibility of $I - K(z)$ to a finite determinant.
steps.detail: Write $F = \sum_{k=1}^N \langle \varphi_k, \cdot \rangle \psi_k$, put $\psi_k(z) = (I - g(z))^{-1}\psi_k$ and $M_{jk}(z) = \delta_{jk} - \langle \varphi_j, \psi_k(z) \rangle$. Solving $(I - K(z))u = h$ means solving $M(z)c = (\langle \varphi_j, h \rangle)_j$ for $c_k = \langle \varphi_k, u \rangle$. So $I - K(z)$ is invertible exactly when the [determinant](c:determinant) $d(z) = \det M(z)$ is nonzero.

steps.slogan: Split the disc into the case $d \equiv 0$ and the case of isolated zeros.
steps.detail: The function $d$ is analytic on the disc $\Omega$. If $d \equiv 0$, then $I - A(z)$ is nowhere invertible on $\Omega$. Otherwise the zeros of $d$ are isolated, the inverse is built from $\mathrm{adj}\,M(z)/d(z)$, so it is [meromorphic](c:meromorphic-function) with finite-rank residues, and at a zero a vector $c \ne 0$ with $M(z)c = 0$ gives the kernel vector $\sum c_k \psi_k(z) \ne 0$.

steps.slogan: Join the local cases over $D$ by connectedness.
steps.detail: Call $z_0$ of type (a) if $I - A(z)$ is nowhere invertible near $z_0$, and of type (b) otherwise. By step 4 both types are open and they cover $D$, so one is empty. In case (b) the exceptional set is locally finite, hence discrete; for $A(z) = zK$ the inverse is the [resolvent](c:resolvent) of $K$ at $1/z$ up to the factor $1/z$.

concepts.c:analytic-family: Analytic dependence on $z$ makes every constructed object analytic in $z$.
concepts.c:compact-operator: Compactness gives the finite-rank approximation that starts the proof.
concepts.c:hilbert-space: Finite-rank approximation of compact operators holds on a Hilbert space.
concepts.c:meromorphic-function: The inverse has poles at the zeros of the determinant and no other singularity.
concepts.c:determinant: The determinant $d(z)$ is the analytic function whose zeros are the exceptional points.
concepts.c:resolvent: For $A(z) = zK$ the inverse is the resolvent of $K$ up to a factor.

source.note: The proof of Reed and Simon, Methods of Modern Mathematical Physics I, theorem VI.14.

statement: In a [closed queueing network](c:closed-queueing-network) of $J$ stations with $N \ge 1$ jobs, exponential servers with state-dependent rates and irreducible routing, a job that arrives at a station in equilibrium sees the other jobs in the stationary distribution $\pi_{N-1}$ of the same network with $N-1$ jobs.

hypotheses.text: The network is a [closed queueing network](c:closed-queueing-network): $N \ge 1$ jobs move among $J$ stations by Markov routing with irreducible matrix $P = (p_{ij})$.
Station $i$ serves at exponential rate $\mu_i(m) > 0$ when $m \ge 1$ jobs are present, so the state $n = (n_1, \dots, n_J)$ is an irreducible [Markov chain](c:markov-chain).

conclusion: For each station $j$ and each $n$ with $\sum_i n_i = N-1$, the long-run probability that an arrival at $j$ finds the other jobs in state $n$ is $\pi_{N-1}(n)$.

proofs.name: Product form and rate balance
proofs.slogan: Write the arrival probability as a ratio of transition rates and cancel it against the product form.
proofs.scope: Every station $j$. For $N = 1$ the network with $0$ jobs is empty, $\pi_0$ is the point mass at the empty state and $G(0) = 1$.

roles.why: Irreducible routing gives positive visit ratios $v_i$, and the traffic equations $v = vP$ drive the sum over source stations.
The exponential servers make the state a Markov chain whose transition rates define the arrival probabilities.

steps.slogan: Write the stationary distribution of the network with $m$ jobs in product form.
steps.detail: By the Gordon-Newell theorem, $\pi_m(n) = G(m)^{-1}\prod_i v_i^{n_i}/\prod_{r=1}^{n_i}\mu_i(r)$ on states with $\sum_i n_i = m$. Here $v$ solves the traffic equations $v_j = \sum_i v_i p_{ij}$ and $G(m)$ normalizes.

steps.slogan: Express the probability seen by an arrival as a ratio of transition rates.
steps.detail: A job reaches station $j$ when a job finishes at some station $i$ and is routed to $j$, so the state moves from $n + e_i$ to $n + e_j$ and the arrival sees $n$. By the ergodic theorem for the [Markov chain](c:markov-chain), the arrival probability is $a_j(n) = \sum_i \pi_N(n+e_i)\mu_i(n_i+1)p_{ij} \big/ \sum_{n'}\sum_i \pi_N(n'+e_i)\mu_i(n'_i+1)p_{ij}$, with $n, n'$ over states of $N-1$ jobs.

steps.slogan: Cancel the service rate against the product form.
steps.detail: In the product form, station $i$ with $n_i + 1$ jobs contributes $v_i^{n_i+1}/\prod_{r \le n_i+1}\mu_i(r)$. Multiplying by $\mu_i(n_i+1)$ leaves $v_i \cdot v_i^{n_i}/\prod_{r \le n_i}\mu_i(r)$. So $\pi_N(n+e_i)\mu_i(n_i+1) = c\,v_i\,\pi_{N-1}(n)$ with $c = G(N-1)/G(N)$.

steps.slogan: Sum over the source stations with the traffic equations.
steps.detail: Step 3 turns the numerator of $a_j(n)$ into $c\,\pi_{N-1}(n)\sum_i v_i p_{ij}$. The traffic equations give $\sum_i v_i p_{ij} = v_j$, so the numerator is $c\,v_j\,\pi_{N-1}(n)$.

steps.slogan: Normalize with $\sum_n \pi_{N-1}(n) = 1$ to get $a_j(n) = \pi_{N-1}(n)$.
steps.detail: The denominator of $a_j(n)$ is the sum of the numerators over $n'$, which is $c\,v_j\sum_{n'}\pi_{N-1}(n') = c\,v_j$. Dividing gives $a_j(n) = \pi_{N-1}(n)$.

concepts.c:closed-queueing-network: The fixed job count $N$ makes the network with $N-1$ jobs a comparable system.
concepts.c:markov-chain: Arrival probabilities are long-run ratios of transition rates of this chain.

source.note: The product-form proof of K. C. Sevcik and I. Mitrani, The distribution of queueing network states at input and output instants, Journal of the ACM 28 (1981), 358-371.

statement: Let $R$ be an excellent [henselian](c:henselian-ring) local ring with [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal) $\mathfrak{m}$ and completion $\hat R$, for example the ring of convergent power series over $\mathbb{C}$. If a system of [polynomial equations](c:algebraic-equation) over $R$ has a solution in $\hat R$, then for each $c$ it has a solution in $R$ congruent to it modulo $\mathfrak{m}^c$.

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is an excellent [henselian](c:henselian-ring) local ring; for convergent power series over $\mathbb{C}$, $\hat R$ is the ring of [formal power series](c:formal-power-series).
The elements $f_1, \dots, f_r \in R[Y_1, \dots, Y_m]$ form a system of [polynomial equations](c:algebraic-equation).
Some $\hat y \in \hat R^m$ satisfies $f(\hat y) = 0$.
The integer $c \ge 1$ is given, and $\mathfrak{m}$ is the [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal) of $R$.

proofs.name: General Néron desingularization
proofs.slogan: Factor the formal solution through a smooth algebra over the ring, then lift a point of that algebra.
proofs.scope: An outline for excellent henselian local rings, following Popescu. Artin proved the case of henselizations of finitely generated algebras over a field or an excellent discrete valuation ring in Publications IHES 36 (1969), 23-58.

roles.why: Excellence makes completion a regular morphism, and the henselian property lifts points of smooth algebras.
The system defines the finitely presented algebra $B = R[Y]/(f)$ that is factored.
The formal solution is the algebra map $B \to \hat R$ that the proof factors and approximates.
The integer $c$ fixes the congruence modulo $\mathfrak{m}^c$ at which the point is lifted.

steps.slogan: Show that the completion map $R \to \hat R$ is a regular morphism.
steps.detail: Excellence of $R$ means that the formal fibers of $R \to \hat R$ are geometrically regular, and completion of a noetherian local ring is flat. So $R \to \hat R$ is a regular morphism of noetherian rings.

steps.slogan: Write the regular morphism as a filtered limit of smooth algebras.
steps.detail: Popescu's general Néron desingularization states that a regular morphism of noetherian rings is a filtered colimit of smooth algebras of finite type. Hence $\hat R = \varinjlim C_\lambda$ with each $C_\lambda$ a smooth $R$-algebra.

steps.slogan: Factor the formal solution through a smooth $R$-algebra.
steps.detail: The solution $\hat y$ is an $R$-algebra map $B = R[Y]/(f) \to \hat R$ from a finitely presented algebra. Finite presentation lets it factor through some $C = C_\lambda$, giving $B \to C \to \hat R$.

steps.slogan: Lift points of the smooth algebra from $R/\mathfrak{m}^c$ to $R$.
steps.detail: For a smooth algebra $C$ over a [henselian](c:henselian-ring) local ring $R$, every point of $C$ over $R/\mathfrak{m}^c$ lifts to an $R$-point, by Hensel's lemma in its smooth form. So $C(R) \to C(R/\mathfrak{m}^c)$ is onto.

steps.slogan: Choose the lifted point that matches the formal solution modulo $\mathfrak{m}^c$.
steps.detail: Reduce $C \to \hat R$ modulo $\mathfrak{m}^c \hat R$ to a point of $C(R/\mathfrak{m}^c)$, using $R/\mathfrak{m}^c = \hat R/\mathfrak{m}^c\hat R$, and lift it to $y_C \in C(R)$. Composing with $B \to C$ gives $y \in R^m$ with $f(y) = 0$ and $y \equiv \hat y \pmod{\mathfrak{m}^c}$.

concepts.c:henselian-ring: Henselian rings let points of smooth algebras lift from the residue ring.
concepts.c:algebraic-equation: The polynomial system defines the algebra whose formal point is approximated.

statement: Let $H$ be a separable infinite-dimensional complex [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) and $\mathrm{Fred}(H)$ the space of [Fredholm operators](c:fredholm-operator) with the norm topology. For every [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space) $X$, the index bundle is a bijection $[X, \mathrm{Fred}(H)] \to K^0(X)$, so $\mathrm{Fred}(H)$ classifies [topological K-theory](c:topological-k-theory).

hypotheses.text: The space $H$ is a separable infinite-dimensional complex [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space), and $\mathrm{Fred}(H)$ has the operator norm topology.
The space $X$ is a [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space).

conclusion: The index bundle $\mathrm{ind}\colon [X, \mathrm{Fred}(H)] \to K^0(X)$ is a bijection, natural in $X$.

proofs.name: Index bundle and Kuiper's theorem
proofs.slogan: Build the index bundle of a family of Fredholm operators and use Kuiper's theorem to show that it is onto and injective.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof. Each step rests on the cited constructions of Atiyah and Jänich; the contractibility of the unitary group is quoted from Kuiper.

roles.why: Infinite dimension and separability make the unitary group contractible and let every bundle embed in $X \times H$.
Compactness gives a finite-dimensional subspace that makes the kernel family a bundle, and gives $K^0(X)$ its definition.

steps.slogan: Trivialize Hilbert bundles over compact spaces using Kuiper's theorem.
steps.detail: The unitary group of $H$ is contractible in the norm topology, so every Hilbert space bundle over a compact space is trivial. Hence a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) of finite rank embeds in $X \times H$ and has a trivial infinite-dimensional complement.

steps.slogan: Construct the index bundle of a family of Fredholm operators.
steps.detail: For a continuous $T\colon X \to \mathrm{Fred}(H)$, compactness gives a finite-dimensional $V \subseteq H$ with $V + \mathrm{im}\,T_x = H$ for all $x$. The spaces $E_x = T_x^{-1}(V)$ form a vector bundle, and $\mathrm{ind}\,T = [E] - [X \times V]$ in $K^0(X)$ does not depend on $V$ or on homotopy.

steps.slogan: Show that every class of $K^0(X)$ is an index.
steps.detail: Write a class as $[E] - [X \times \mathbb{C}^m]$. By step 1, $E^\perp \cong X \times H$ for the complement $E^\perp$, so the projection onto $E^\perp$ composed with this trivialization is a family with kernel bundle $E$ and index $[E]$. Composing with a constant Fredholm operator of index $-m$ gives the class.

steps.slogan: Show that families with the same index are homotopic.
steps.detail: If $\mathrm{ind}\,T = \mathrm{ind}\,T'$, stabilize both by trivial finite-dimensional pieces until their kernel bundles are isomorphic and their cokernels vanish. By Kuiper the isomorphisms between the remaining trivial Hilbert bundles form a contractible space, so $T$ and $T'$ are homotopic through Fredholm families.

steps.slogan: Combine the two steps into a natural bijection and a classifying space.
steps.detail: Steps 2 to 4 show that $\mathrm{ind}$ is well defined, onto and injective, and it commutes with pullback along maps $X' \to X$. So $\mathrm{Fred}(H)$ represents the functor $K^0$ on compact spaces, that is, it classifies [topological K-theory](c:topological-k-theory).

concepts.c:hilbert-space: The Hilbert space supplies the Fredholm operators and the contractible unitary group.
concepts.c:compact-hausdorff-space: Compact test spaces are where the K-theory group and the index bundle are defined.
concepts.c:fredholm-operator: Fredholm operators have finite kernel and cokernel, so families give virtual bundles.
concepts.c:topological-k-theory: The bijection identifies homotopy classes of maps with the K-theory group.
concepts.c:vector-bundle: The index bundle and the classes of $K^0(X)$ are made of vector bundles.

source.ref: M. F. Atiyah, K-Theory, W. A. Benjamin, New York, 1967, Appendix (Theorem A1); K. Jänich, Vektorraumbündel und der Raum der Fredholm-Operatoren, Mathematische Annalen 161 (1965), 129-142
source.note: Atiyah gives the index bundle and the proof of bijectivity from Kuiper's theorem; Jänich proves the theorem independently.

statement: Let $b\colon U \times V \to \mathbb{R}$ be a bounded [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) on real [Hilbert spaces](c:hilbert-space) that satisfies the [inf-sup condition](c:inf-sup-condition) with constant $\gamma > 0$ and is nondegenerate in $v$. Then each $f \in V^*$ gives a unique $u \in U$ with $b(u, \cdot) = f$, and $\|u\| \le \|f\|/\gamma$.

hypotheses.text: The spaces $U$ and $V$ are real [Hilbert spaces](c:hilbert-space).
The map $b\colon U \times V \to \mathbb{R}$ is a [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) with $|b(u,v)| \le M\|u\|\|v\|$.
For some $\gamma > 0$, the [inf-sup condition](c:inf-sup-condition) $\sup_{\|v\| \le 1} |b(u,v)| \ge \gamma\|u\|$ holds for all $u \in U$.
For every $v \ne 0$ in $V$, some $u \in U$ has $b(u,v) \ne 0$.

conclusion: For each $f \in V^*$ there is a unique $u \in U$ with $b(u,v) = f(v)$ for all $v \in V$, and $\|u\| \le \|f\|/\gamma$.

proofs.name: Bounded below with dense range
proofs.slogan: Turn the form into an operator that is bounded below and has dense range, hence is invertible.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for real spaces. The zero data $f = 0$ gives $u = 0$ by the same argument.

roles.why: Completeness of $U$ makes the range closed, and reflexivity of $V$ identifies functionals on $V^*$ with elements of $V$.
Boundedness of $b$ makes $A$ a bounded operator into $V^*$.
The inf-sup bound is the lower bound $\|Au\| \ge \gamma\|u\|$.
Nondegeneracy in $v$ excludes a nonzero functional that annihilates the range.

steps.slogan: Turn $b$ into a bounded operator $A\colon U \to V^*$.
steps.detail: Put $(Au)(v) = b(u,v)$, with values in the [dual space](c:dual-space) $V^*$. Boundedness of $b$ gives $\|Au\| \le M\|u\|$. The claim becomes that $A$ is bijective with $\|A^{-1}\| \le 1/\gamma$.

steps.slogan: Show that $A$ is bounded below, hence injective with closed range.
steps.detail: The inf-sup condition reads $\|Au\| \ge \gamma\|u\|$, so $A$ is injective. If $Au_k$ converges, then $(u_k)$ is Cauchy, so it converges in the complete space $U$, and the limit of $Au_k$ lies in the range. Hence the range is closed.

steps.slogan: Show that the range of $A$ is dense, using reflexivity and nondegeneracy.
steps.detail: If the range is not dense, the Hahn-Banach theorem gives a nonzero functional on $V^*$ that vanishes on it. Since a Hilbert space is reflexive, this functional is evaluation at some $v \ne 0$. Then $b(u,v) = 0$ for all $u$, which contradicts nondegeneracy.

steps.slogan: Conclude existence, uniqueness and the bound with $u = A^{-1}f$.
steps.detail: A closed and dense range is all of $V^*$, so $A$ is onto, and with injectivity it is bijective. Then $u = A^{-1}f$ is the unique solution of $b(u, \cdot) = f$, and $\|u\| \le \|f\|/\gamma$ follows from $\|Au\| \ge \gamma\|u\|$.

concepts.c:hilbert-space: Completeness and reflexivity of the spaces drive the closed range and density steps.
concepts.c:bilinear-form: The bilinear form defines the operator that the proof inverts.
concepts.c:inf-sup-condition: The inf-sup condition is the lower bound that gives injectivity and stability.
concepts.c:dual-space: The operator $A$ takes values in the dual space of $V$.

source.note: The standard proof of the Banach-Nečas-Babuška theorem, as in Ern and Guermond, Theory and Practice of Finite Elements, section 2.1; the form of the result is due to Babuška, Numerische Mathematik 16 (1971), 322-333.
